intro: On the eastern shore of Lake Van, in Van province, rises Ayanis Fortress, an ancient city of the 7th century BC. This Urartian fortress was built by King Rusa II, and today it is famous for its exceptionally well-preserved Temple of Haldi. Let us step into its story.
history: Its story begins around 673/2 BC, when Rusa II founded it as 'Rusahinili opposite Mount Eiduru'. Yet it did not last long. In the mid-7th century BC an earthquake and fire struck, and the fortress was abandoned. Here lies the paradox of Ayanis: the very collapse that ended it effectively sealed the site, and that is why its temple walls, inscriptions and bronze weapons are so remarkably preserved.
structure-2: You are now standing in the colonnaded hall, a wide hall divided by rows of columns. Pause for a moment and picture those rows rising around you.
structure-4: Now look at the city walls. Built of andesite blocks, these sturdy walls tell you at a glance how seriously this fortress took its defence.
structure-5: And here is the foundation inscription. Its words record by whom and when the structure was built: a builder's signature, carved in stone.
highlights: As you wander, don't miss the Temple of Haldi, and be sure to seek out the storage magazines as well.
facts: Did you know? One of the longest Urartian inscriptions survives on the temple façade: the long cuneiform text on the wall of the Temple of Haldi tells the fortress's founding in the king's own words. The lion-headed bronze shield found in 1997 is the first example of its kind ever recovered in excavation. And because Rusa II built the fortress in one campaign in the seventh century BC, and it was destroyed soon after, Ayanis is a single-period time capsule.
outro: Here our tour of Ayanis Fortress comes to an end. Before you go, please leave the stones untouched, keep to the marked paths and carry water with you. These walls kept their secrets for a very long time; help them keep them for those who come after you. Enjoy your visit.
